880.tone: Koffi 2022 (native-speaker phonetician): Anyi uses F0 lexically (H vs L; Appendix 1 lists ~60 pitch-based minimal pairs + 14 triplets from a 4,539-word corpus, e.g. <ajaá> 'marriage' vs <ajáa> 'inheritance', <anυnmáa> 'yesterday' vs <anυnmaán> 'grand child'; 'The low tone is unmarked. Il n'y a pas en agni d'intonation musicale, comme il en existe en certaines langues africaines, en yorouba (ou nago) par exemple » followed by the vowel-quality accent rules in; Koffi 2022:66,76 reads Delafosse's 'accent' rules as the grammatical pitch rules. Quaireau 1978/1987 and Burmeister 1983 (cited by Koffi, not reached) treat Anyi as tonal with few minimal pairs.

882.tone: Post & Kanno 2013: two lexically specified underlying tones (H, L) per morpheme; surface word contours level-high / low(-falling) / rising; final heavy syllable (CVV, CVN/nasalized V, CVʔ, CVC) forces a rising contour in isolation, underlying tone then recoverable from spreading onto a following clitic (ke 'IND'); bimoraic word-minimality constraint. Abraham 1985 instead lists three tonemes (rising, level, falling). Neither source mentions stress or accentual prominence at all; the verdict is TONAL (silence on stress), not an explicit denial of word stress.

884.dq: In basic roots, primary stress is normally applied to the penultimate syllable of a word. ... [§2.8] This is because sentence-level stress in Abma is not yet understood. Stress marking therefore reflects only what is heard, rather than the underlying phonological system.

884.heavy: Long vowels take stress, regardless of their position in the word; words ending in closed syllables typically receive word-final stress; where both occur, long vowels take precedence. §3.1.2.2: long syllables and closed syllables are stressed, regardless of their position in the word.
884.prule: Basic roots: primary stress on the penultimate syllable by default; quantity-sensitive override: a long vowel is stressed wherever it occurs in the word; a word ending in a closed syllable takes final stress; when both occur, the long vowel wins (scale CVV > final CVC > CV). Multimorphemic words assumed penultimate with alternating secondaries, but author says stress beyond the root is 'not straightforward'.
884.srule: Secondary stress on every alternate syllable to the left of the penultimate (primary) syllable, e.g. /,ma.ri.'bu.ku/ 'humpback snapper'; assumed to hold in multimorphemic words as well ('each alternating syllable to the left also being stressed').

887.prule: No positional stress rule. Prominence is a pitch accent (high vs. normal pitch, plus falling pitch on long vowels/diphthongs) that is part of the underlying form of each morpheme and is not synchronically predictable; it is contrastive (minimal pairs exist but are not pervasive). Surface word contours follow from word-level redistribution rules (no adjacent accented syllables) and grammatical accent shifts (mostly one syllable rightward) under derivation/inflection. The authors explicitly reject an alternating-syllable (rhythmic) analysis.

887.tone: Cowell & Moss describe Arapaho as having a pitch accent system: high pitch (acute) vs. normal (unmarked) pitch, with a falling high-to-normal pitch on long vowels and diphthongs only; accent is lexically specified per morpheme ('not predictable (at least synchronically)'), contrastive ('pitch accents are contrastive, and other minimal pairs occur') but 'certainly not equivalent to tonal systems in languages such as Mandarin Chinese'. No separate stress rule is given; the word 'stress' appears in the phonology chapter only incidentally. Secondary literature (Bogomolets 2014 CU Boulder MA 'Acoustic correlates of Arapaho prominence'; Bogomolets 2023 'Accent and tone in Arapaho, Plains Algonquian', OUP) argues the system behaves like morpho-lexical accent rather than pitch accent (short accented vowels: higher F0 and amplitude; long: longer duration) (Bogomolets 2014: abstract, p. iii; Bogomolets 2023: sec. 7.1 p. 219 'best analyzed as a lexical accent system', sec. 7.2.1 p. 227 on the acoustic correlates).

889.prule: No simplex word-stress position is stated anywhere in the monograph. Åström explicitly leaves the musical (tonal) accent undescribed (§5) and files everything he does say under the EXPIRATORY accent (§6): non-compound trisyllables 'allmänneligen samma aksent som uti rspr.' (accent referred to Standard Swedish, left unmarked); then, 'keeping an old terminology', akut on historically monosyllabic words (plus most disyllabic personal names and a few compounds), gravis (the unmarked majority) on original disyllables and on trisyllables reduced to disyllables, cirkumflex (two-peaked) on original disyllables apocopated to monosyllables. Root-syllable main stress is presupposed throughout ('fullt betonad' vs 'svagare betonad stafvelse' §4; 'rotstafvelse' vs 'obetonad stafvelse' §74; words that 'icke uppbar hufvudton'; exceptional 'slutbetoning'/'ultimabetoning' §74 Anm. 3-4; historical 'ändelsebetoning' §10) but is never stated as a placement rule, so nothing computable from syllable count or weight is given.
889.srule: Rule given (Lindgren 1890, Burträsk): stress grades are fortis / strong or weak semifortis / levis / unstressed (§8); in accent-2 words the weak secondary stress (levis) falls on the final syllable whatever syllable carries the main stress (§12 Anm. 1), shifting onto a following weakly stressed word in connected speech (§12 Anm. 2); strong semifortis falls on the accent syllable of the second member of compounds (§15) and on the formerly main-stressed syllable of re-accented loanwords (§13 mom. 6). Åström 1888 (Degerfors) mentions 'biaksent'/'biton' only in passing (§1 Anm. 4 p. 8; §72 Anm. 3 p. 77).

889.tone: Åström (§5) 'kan icke nöjaktigt redogöra' for the musical (pitch) accent and leaves it 'obeaktad ock obetecknad'; under the heading of the EXPIRATORY accent (§6) he classifies every word, 'med bibehållande af en gammal terminologi', as akut / gravis / cirkumflex -- the Kock-era labels for what is now analysed as the North Germanic tonal accent 1 / accent 2 opposition plus the Norrlandic two-peaked circumflex on apocopated old long-stem disyllables (second half rising before a 'long' consonant, else falling; lost in compounds and in connected speech unless sentence-final or emphasised, §6 Anm. 1). sv/en Wikipedia 'Norrländska mål'/'Norrland dialects' likewise report apocope 'med bevarad tvåtoppig ordaccent (så kallad cirkumflex accent)'. This is a Germanic dynamic-stress language with a lexical word-accent overlay, not a stressless pitch-accent system: the monograph is organised as 'Sonanterna i betonad stafvelse' vs 'i obetonad stafvelse' (root syllable vs ending), speaks of 'fullt betonad' vs 'svagare betonad stafvelse' (§4), of vowels that 'icke uppbär hufvudton', and of exceptional 'slutbetoning'/'ultimabetoning' (§74 Anm. 3-4) and historical 'ändelsebetoning'.

890.dq: A sesqui-syllable is composed of a main syllable C V (C) preceded by a pre-syllable C-. The main syllable is identical to a monosyllable. The pre-syllable is short and unstressed, without distinctive vowel, and its consonantal system is reduced.
890.dloc: sec. 2.1 'Syllabic structure' (p.2) and sec. 2.2 'Voice-type register system of Arem' (p.3)
890.prule: Word = monosyllable CV(C) or sesquisyllable C-CV(C) (Arem retains 55-60% sesquisyllables, the highest in Vietic). Ferlus: 'The pre-syllable is short and unstressed, without distinctive vowel, and its consonantal system is reduced. A pre-syllable can not exist alone.' Hence in every disyllabic (sesquisyllabic) word stress falls on the main = final syllable; no longer non-compound words are described, so the grid is fixed only at length 2. Independently of stress, the main-syllable rhyme carries a voice-type register contrast (series 1 high-clear vs series 2 low-breathy) crossed with modal~glottalized in voiced-final rhymes, which Ferlus analyses as 'a four tones system' (a, aˀ, à, àˀ, matched to Vietnamese ngang/sắc/huyền/nặng); -h and stop-checked rhymes occur in both sets.
890.srule: Not mentioned in Ferlus 2014 (sec. 2 'Phonetic system', pp.2-5, read in full; the only stress statement is that the pre-syllable of a sesquisyllable is unstressed, and no word longer than a sesquisyllable is described). 895.heavy: a heavy syllable (a closed syllable) vs. light (an open syllable)
895.prule: Primary prominence on the first syllable of a (non-compounded) word, unless the first syllable is light (open) and the second is heavy (closed), in which case it falls on the second; never beyond the second syllable.
895.srule: Secondary prominence from left-to-right moraic trochees (Mahanta 2001): in a run of light (open) syllables it falls on every odd-numbered syllable from the left after the primary ((ˈLL)(ˌLL), (ˈLL)(ˌLL)L, (ˈLL)(ˌLL)(ˌLL)); a heavy (closed) syllable is prominent unless the preceding syllable is prominent (adjacent stresses prohibited, the clashing syllable left unfooted), so in trisyllables only a final heavy syllable carries secondary prominence ((LL)(H), (H)L(H); none in (LL)L, L(H)L, (H)HL). Not mentioned in the JIPA 2012 illustration itself; Mahanta 2001 flags the secondary pattern as intuition-based ('our claims for secondary prominence need more evidence', p.69).

tn.translation: The accentuation is not transmitted in the Avesta; but from some phenomena one may surmise that it originally agreed in general with that of Old Indic, although the expiratory element seems gradually to have become predominant. ... 1. 904.prule: Lexical/grammatical tone system: three level tones (H, M, L) plus Rising on short vowels, all nine two-tone combinations attested on disyllabic nouns; verbs fall into tone classes with construction-dependent tone rules. No word-stress rule is stated in either reachable source; the words 'stress'/'accent' do not occur in Kilpatrick & Gilley 2004.
904.srule: Not mentioned in Kilpatrick & Gilley 2004 (whole article, pp. 235-260, read) nor in Kilpatrick 2004 (OPSL 9, pp. 85-91) or Callinan 1981 (OPSL 1, pp. 64-73): all three describe Avokaya prosody as tone only (three level tones H/M/L, one tone per syllable) and say nothing about word stress, primary or secondary.
904.quote: The nominal system of Avokaya demonstrates three level tone patterns, High, Mid and Low. In addition, there is a Rising contour on short vowels, but no Falling contour on short vowels. Phonetically a Falling or Rising contour may occur on long vowels, but these long vowels are considered sequences of two Tone Bearing Units (TBU). ... In the nominal system, there are no restrictions on the occurrence of the three level tones, as shown by the representative examples below. (1) Monosyllabic nouns H ... M ... L ... (2) Disyllabic nouns HH ... HM ... HL ... MH ... MM ... ML ... LH ... LM ... LL ..…
904.loc: Kilpatrick & Gilley 2004, sec. 1 Introduction, pp. 235-236; Kilpatrick 2004 OPSL 9, 'Tones', p. 88
904.idn: Avokaya (an unnamed dialect 'spoken in southern Sudan'); data: southern Sudan; data gathered over approximately 23 years of work in the language (paper published 2004); speakers/villages not stated
904.tone: Three level tones H/M/L contrast freely on nouns (pa 'leg' H, fE 'tree' M, fa 'bone' L; all 9 patterns on disyllables); Rising contour restricted to word-initial short syllables ('could be analyzed as right-to-left association of tone'); Falling only on long vowels (= two TBUs); verbs have 4 tone classes (M, MM, L, ML) with ordered tone rules differing between SVO and SOV constructions; HL merges to M in the verbal system. Stress/accent is never mentioned.

905.prule: Default ('radical') accent on the first syllable of di- and trisyllables; a second, 'shifting' accent falls on suffixal 'particles' according to morphological category: descriptive-noun derivatives (-kan, -ngel) accent the final syllable; present/past tense verbs accent the tense-marking portion; future tenses accent the penult regardless of length; present participles accent the final; past participles the penult; the stative participial form the antepenult.
